Question 1
?

If X1∼N(−1,62) and X2∼N(5,82) are independent, then what is the distribution of Y=X2−X1?

a
N(−6,122)
b
Not enough information to determine the answer
c
N(6,102)
d
N(−6,102)
e
N(6,122)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X1 and X2 are independent random variables, where X1∼N(μ1,σ12) and X2∼N(μ2,σ22), then

X2−X1∼N(μ2−μ1,σ12+σ22).

Since X1 and X2 are independent, we have

Y=X2−X1∼N(5−(−1),62+82)∼N(6,100)∼N(6,102).

Therefore, Y∼N(6,102).

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2} & ∼N(7+(-2),16+4) \\  & ∼N(5,20).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $Y∼N(5,20).$

$$

q-109661.name: Question 8
q-109661.problem: If ${X}_{1}∼N(-2,1)$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(-3,10)$ are independent, then what is the distribution of $Y=3{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2}?$
q-109661.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2} & ∼N(3\cdot (-2)+(-2)\cdot (-3),{3}^{2}\cdot 1+(-2)^{2}\cdot 10) \\  & ∼N(0,49).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y∼N(0,49).$

q-109673.name: Question 11
q-109673.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=2{X}_{1}-3{X}_{2} & ∼N(2{\mu }_{1}-3{\mu }_{2},{2}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20-15,4\cdot 16+9\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(5,100).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =5$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{100}=10.$ 

We want to find $P(Y\ge 10).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 25) & =P(Z\ge \frac{10-5}{10}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.5) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.5) \\  & =1-Φ(0.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.5)≈0.6915.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 10) & =1-Φ(0.5) \\  & =1-0.6915 \\  & ≈0.31.\end{aligned}
$$

A particular shop sells chicken eggs and quail eggs. Let $X$ denote the weight of a chicken egg, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a quail egg. We want to find

P(X>5Y)=P(X-5Y>0).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}X-5Y & ∼N(64-5\cdot 14,25+{5}^{2}\cdot 1) \\  & ∼N(-6,50).\end{aligned}

So, the variable $X-5Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-6$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{50}.$

In order to find $P(X-5Y>0),$ we convert $X-5Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-5Y>0) & =P(Z>\frac{0+6}{\sqrt{50}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.85) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.85) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.85) \\  & =1-Φ(0.85)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the weight of a chicken egg is more than $5$ times greater than the weight of a quail egg is $0.1977.$

The amount of soda in one can is normally distributed with a mean of $340\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $4\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weight of a can is normally distributed with a mean of $25\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $1\,{\text{g}}^{2}$ If one can containing soda is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $360\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights of soda and cans are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-2.3\,$ | $\,0.0102\,$ | $\,0.0099\,$ | $\,0.0096\,$ | $\,0.0094\,$ |
| $\,-2.2\,$ | $\,0.0132\,$ | $\,0.0129\,$ | $\,0.0125\,$ | $\,0.0122\,$ |
| $\,-2.1\,$ | $\,0.0170\,$ | $\,0.0166\,$ | $\,0.0162\,$ | $\,0.0158\,$ |
q-109750.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the weight of the soda, and let $Y$ denote the weight of the can. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>360).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(340,4)$ and $Y∼N(25,1)$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(340+25,4+1) \\  & ∼N(365,5).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =365$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{5}.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>360),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>360) & =P(Z>\frac{360-365}{\sqrt{5}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-2.24) \\  & =1-P(Z\le -2.24) \\  & =1-Φ(-2.24)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-2.24)≈0.0125.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>360) & ≈1-Φ(-2.24) \\  & ≈1-0.0125 \\  & ≈0.9875.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that a randomly selected can with soda weighs more than $360$ grams is $0.9875.$

$$

$$

$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-Y<0) & ≈Φ(-0.94) \\  & ≈0.1736.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110056.problem:
The volumes of some chocolate muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $57\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{ml}.$ The volumes of some pumpkin muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $42\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{ml}.$  During cooking, it is known that chocolate muffins double in volume, while pumpkin muffins triple in volume.

If a chocolate muffin and a  pumpkin muffin are randomly selected after cooking, what is the probability that the sum of their volumes is more than $240\,\text{ml}$ but less than $250\,\text{ml}?$ You may assume that the volumes of the muffins are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ | $\,0.9788\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9861\,$ | $\,0.9864\,$ | $\,0.9868\,$ | $\,0.9871\,$ | $\,0.9875\,$ |
q-110056.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the volume of a chocolate muffin before cooking, and let $Y$ denote the volume of a pumpkin muffin before cooking. We want to find 

$$
P(240<2X+3Y<250).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(57,{2}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(42,{1}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}2X+3Y & ∼N(2\cdot 57+3\cdot 42,{2}^{2}\cdot {2}^{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot 1) \\  & ∼N(240,25).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $2X+3Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =240$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{25}=5.$

In order to find $P(100<2X+3Y<120),$ we convert $2X+3Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(240<2X+3Y<250) & =P(\frac{240-240}{5}<Z<\frac{250-240}{5}) \\  & =P(0<Z<2) \\  & =P(Z<2)-P(Z\le 0) \\  & =P(Z\le 2)-P(Z\le 0) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(0)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(2) & ≈0.9772,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(240<2X+3Y<250) & =Φ(2)-Φ(0) \\  & ≈0.9772-0.5 \\  & =0.4772.\end{aligned}
$$

The results of a group of students on an algebra test are normally distributed with a mean of $75$ and a variance of $125$, while the results of the same group on a geometry test are normally distributed with a mean of $62$ and a variance of $110.$ 
If one student is randomly selected, what is the probability that they scored higher on the algebra test? You may assume that the student's scores on both tests are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.2005\,$ | $\,0.1977\,$ | $\,0.1949\,$ | $\,0.1922\,$ | $\,0.1894\,$ |
| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2296\,$ | $\,0.2266\,$ | $\,0.2236\,$ | $\,0.2206\,$ | $\,0.2177\,$ |
| $\,-0.6\,$ | $\,0.2611\,$ | $\,0.2578\,$ | $\,0.2546\,$ | $\,0.2514\,$ | $\,0.2483\,$ |
q-108976.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the student's algebra test result, and let $Y$ denote the student's geometry result. We want to find 

$$
P(X>Y)=P(X-Y>0).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(75,125)$ and $Y∼N(62,110)$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X-Y & ∼N(75-62,125+110) \\  & ∼N(13,235).\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the variable $X-Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =13$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{235}.$

In order to find $P(X-Y>0),$ we convert $X-Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:
    

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-Y>0) & =P(Z>\frac{0-13}{\sqrt{235}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-0.85) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.85)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-0.85)≈0.1977.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-Y>0) & ≈1-Φ(-0.85) \\  & ≈1-0.1977 \\  & =0.8023.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the student scored higher on the algebra test is $0.8023.$
